lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Well, Alexander — you can hardly deny you're my son now. If you were actually Ammon's boy, you wouldn't be dead.
lines.note: Opening line lands flat and dry. Philip is not cruel; he is simply right.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I knew perfectly well I was your son, Father — Philip's son, Amyntas's grandson. I just accepted the oracle because I thought it would be useful.
lines.note: Alexander's defence is immediate and practical. He's not embarrassed; he's managing.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Useful. You thought it was useful to let priests make a fool of you.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Not like that. The barbarians were terrified of me — nobody wanted to fight a god. It made the conquests easier.
lines.note: Still managing. He believes this argument.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And what conquests, exactly? You were fighting cowards. Their idea of arms was a little bow, a little wicker shield, a screen of woven osiers. [pause] Beating Greeks — that would have been something. Boeotians, Phocians, Athenians. The Arcadian heavy infantry. The Thessalian cavalry. The javelin-men of Elis, the light troops of Mantinea. Or Thracians, Illyrians, Paeonians — those are real victories. Medes and Persians and Chaldaeans? Gold-draped, perfumed, soft men who'd already run from ten thousand Greeks under Clearchus — run before the arrows even reached them. You know that. Everyone knows that.
lines.note: Philip builds steam here. The list of Greeks is slightly proud — these were his own people — and the contempt for Persians is genuine.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: The Scythians weren't soft, Father. And the Indian elephants. I didn't win those by bribery or by splitting their forces — I beat them straight. I never broke an oath, never made a promise I didn't keep, never did anything dishonest for the sake of a victory. And the Greek states — most of them I brought over without bloodshed. As for the Thebans — I think you know what I did to Thebes.
lines.note: Alexander is making a real case. There's some defensiveness but also genuine pride. He believes this.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I know all of it. Cleitus told me. The Cleitus you ran through with a spear at dinner — because he had the nerve to praise me in front of you.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And then there's the rest of it. You threw off the Macedonian cloak and put on a Persian robe, a kandys — an upright tiara. You expected free men, Macedonians, to prostrate themselves before you. And the most ridiculous part: you were imitating the people you'd beaten. I won't even start on the rest — locking educated men in cages with lions, the marriages you contracted, the extraordinary devotion to Hephaestion. [pause] There was one thing I approved of when I heard it: that you kept your hands off Darius's wife, beautiful as she was, and treated his mother and daughters with proper care. That, at least, was kingly.
lines.note: Philip is doing something subtle here: he ends with the one genuine compliment, which lands harder than more criticism would.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And the courage, Father? Doesn't that count? Jumping down first inside the walls at the Oxydracae, alone? Taking those wounds?
lines.note: Alexander is reaching now. He knows the previous charges landed.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I don't praise that either — not because I think it's wrong for a king to take risks ahead of his men, but because it was exactly wrong for you. You were claiming to be a god. So when you got wounded — when they watched you carried off the battlefield, bleeding, crying out from the pain — what was that? It was a joke. Ammon exposed as a fraud, his prophets exposed as flatterers. Who wouldn't laugh, watching the son of Zeus nearly faint and calling for the doctors? [pause] And now that you're dead — do you really think people aren't mocking the whole performance? Looking at the god's corpse stretched out, already bloating and rotting like every other body ever made? And another thing: this 'usefulness' you keep mentioning — winning easily because they thought you were divine — that actually diminished every achievement. If a god did it, what was the glory? It counts for nothing.
lines.note: Philip's longest speech. It builds from tactical observation to something genuinely damning. The image of the bloating corpse is delivered as a plain fact.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Humanity doesn't see it that way. They rank me alongside Heracles and Dionysus. And that rock, Aornus — neither of them ever took it. I did.
lines.note: Alexander is not giving up. He means this. The comparison to Heracles and Dionysus is not parody; it's sincere, which makes it sadder.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Do you hear yourself? You're doing it again — comparing yourself to Heracles and Dionysus. That's Ammon's son talking, not mine. [pause] Alexander. Aren't you ashamed? Can you not put down the puffery, even now? You're dead. You know that, don't you? You do understand that you're dead.
lines.note: The last line is not rhetorical. Philip genuinely wants an answer, and the wanting is what makes it land.
